vtrmc-1994-01.title: Change the order of integration
vtrmc-1994-01.body:
The integrand does not depend on $y$, and $\int_0^x dy=x$, so
$$I=\int_0^1\int_0^{1-x^2}x\,e^{(1-z)^2}\,dz\,dx.$$
The region $0\le x\le1$, $0\le z\le1-x^2$ is also $0\le z\le1$, $0\le x\le\sqrt{1-z}$. Swapping the order,
$$I=\int_0^1e^{(1-z)^2}\int_0^{\sqrt{1-z}}x\,dx\,dz=\int_0^1\frac{1-z}{2}\,e^{(1-z)^2}\,dz=\Bigl[-\tfrac14e^{(1-z)^2}\Bigr]_0^1=\frac{e-1}{4}.$$

**Answer:** $\frac{e-1}4\approx0.42957$.

vtrmc-1994-01.title: Integrate by parts in $x$
vtrmc-1994-01.body:
After the $y$-integration, $I=\int_0^1x\,H(x)\,dx$ with $H(x)=\int_0^{1-x^2}e^{(1-z)^2}dz$. Then $H(1)=0$ and $H'(x)=-2x\,e^{(x^2)^2}=-2xe^{x^4}$. Integrating by parts with $\frac{x^2}{2}$ as antiderivative of $x$:
$$I=\Bigl[\tfrac{x^2}{2}H(x)\Bigr]_0^1-\int_0^1\frac{x^2}{2}H'(x)\,dx=\int_0^1x^3e^{x^4}\,dx=\Bigl[\tfrac14e^{x^4}\Bigr]_0^1=\frac{e-1}4.$$
(A numerical triple integration gives $0.429570$.)

**Answer:** $\frac{e-1}4$.

vtrmc-1994-02.title: An identity, then minimise in $y$
vtrmc-1994-02.body:
$g$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $[0,f(a)]$ with $g(0)=0$ (the inverse of a continuous strictly increasing function on an interval). Let $F(x)=\int_0^xf$ and $G(y)=\int_0^yg$.

**Step 1: $F(x)+G(f(x))=xf(x)$ for $0\le x\le a$.** Consider the rectangle $R=[0,x]\times[0,f(x)]$ in the $(s,t)$-plane and the sets
$$S_1=\{(s,t)\in R:\ t<f(s)\},\qquad S_2=\{(s,t)\in R:\ s<g(t)\}.$$
By Fubini, the area of $S_1$ is $\int_0^xf(s)\,ds=F(x)$ and the area of $S_2$ is $\int_0^{f(x)}g(t)\,dt=G(f(x))$. Since $f$ is strictly increasing, $t<f(s)\iff g(t)<s$, so $S_1$ and $S_2$ are disjoint, and every point of $R$ not on the graph $t=f(s)$ lies in one of them. The graph of a continuous function has area zero, so $F(x)+G(f(x))=\operatorname{area}(R)=xf(x)$.

**Step 2.** Fix $x\in[0,a]$ and let $\varphi(y)=F(x)+G(y)-xy$ for $y\in[0,f(a)]$. By the fundamental theorem of calculus $\varphi'(y)=g(y)-x$, which is negative for $y<f(x)$ and positive for $y>f(x)$ (as $g$ is increasing and $g(f(x))=x$). So $\varphi$ is smallest at $y=f(x)$, and by Step 1, $\varphi(f(x))=0$. Hence $\varphi(y)\ge0$, i.e.
$$xy\le\int_0^xf(t)\,dt+\int_0^yg(t)\,dt.\ ∎$$

vtrmc-1994-02.title: Areas in a picture (official idea)
vtrmc-1994-02.body:
Draw the graph of $f$ on $[0,a]$ and the rectangle $[0,x]\times[0,y]$ of area $xy$.
- $\int_0^xf(t)\,dt$ is the area $C$ under the graph over $[0,x]$.
- $\int_0^yg(t)\,dt$ is the area between the graph and the vertical axis for heights in $[0,y]$ (the graph of $g$ is the graph of $f$ reflected in the line $t=s$).

If $y\ge f(x)$, the rectangle is covered by the region under the graph over $[0,x]$ (area $C$) together with the region to the left of the graph for heights in $[0,y]$; the latter also contains an extra piece $B$ to the right of $s=x$ (for heights between $f(x)$ and $y$). So $xy\le C+(\text{area }A)+B$ where $A\cup B$ is the area left of the graph, i.e. $xy\le\int_0^xf+\int_0^yg$. If $y\le f(x)$, swap the roles of $f$ and $g$ (reflect the picture in the diagonal). Step 1 of the first solution turns this picture into a rigorous argument. ∎

vtrmc-1994-03.title: Reduce to $f'=f\pm f^2$ and solve for $1/f$
vtrmc-1994-03.body:
**Reduction.** Differentiating (the integrand is continuous) gives $2ff'=f^2-f^4+f'^2$, i.e.
$$(f'-f)^2=f'^2-2ff'+f^2=f^4. \tag{1}$$
Conversely, if $f$ is $C^1$ with (1) and $f(0)^2=100$, then $\frac{d}{dx}f^2=2ff'=f^2-f^4+f'^2$, and integrating from $0$ gives the original equation. So we must solve (1) with $f(0)=\pm10$.

**The sign is constant.** On any interval where $f\ne0$, the function $\varepsilon=\frac{f'-f}{f^2}$ is continuous and by (1) takes only the values $\pm1$, so it is constant there. Let $J$ be the largest interval containing $0$ on which $f\ne0$. On $J$, $f'=f+\varepsilon f^2$ for a fixed $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$.

**Solving.** Put $u=1/f$ on $J$. Then $u'=-\frac{f'}{f^2}=-\frac1f-\varepsilon=-u-\varepsilon$, so $(e^xu)'=-\varepsilon e^x$ and
$$u(x)=-\varepsilon+\bigl(u(0)+\varepsilon\bigr)e^{-x},\qquad u(0)=\pm\tfrac1{10}.$$
This $u$ is finite everywhere, so $f=1/u$ cannot tend to $0$ at an end of $J$; by continuity $f$ never vanishes and $J$ is the whole interval of definition. The four cases:
- $f(0)=10$, $\varepsilon=1$: $u(0)+\varepsilon=\frac{11}{10}$, so $u=\frac{11e^{-x}-10}{10}$ and $f=\dfrac{10}{11e^{-x}-10}=\dfrac{-10}{10-11e^{-x}}$ (at $x=0$: $\frac{-10}{-1}=10$ ✓).
- $f(0)=10$, $\varepsilon=-1$: $u=1-\frac9{10}e^{-x}$, $f=\dfrac{10}{10-9e^{-x}}$.
- $f(0)=-10$, $\varepsilon=1$: $u=-1+\frac9{10}e^{-x}$, $f=\dfrac{-10}{10-9e^{-x}}$.
- $f(0)=-10$, $\varepsilon=-1$: $u=1-\frac{11}{10}e^{-x}$, $f=\dfrac{10}{10-11e^{-x}}$ (at $x=0$: $\frac{10}{-1}=-10$ ✓).

Each satisfies (1) (by reversing the computation) and hence the original equation. The functions $\pm\frac{10}{10-9e^{-x}}$ are defined for $x>\ln\frac9{10}$ and $\pm\frac{10}{10-11e^{-x}}$ for $x<\ln\frac{11}{10}$ (they blow up at the excluded point). A numerical check of the integral equation for all four functions at $x=0.05$ confirms them.

**Answer:** $f(x)=\pm\dfrac{10}{10-9e^{-x}}$ or $f(x)=\pm\dfrac{10}{10-11e^{-x}}$.

vtrmc-1994-04.title: Solve for $b$ and compare with $-\tfrac12$
vtrmc-1994-04.body:
Let $x>0$ be a root. Solving the equation for $b$ (note $x^3+x>0$):
$$b=-\frac{a(x^4+1)+x^2}{x^3+x}.$$
Then
$$a+b=\frac{a(x^3+x)-a(x^4+1)-x^2}{x(x^2+1)}=\frac{-a(x-1)^2(x^2+x+1)-x^2}{x(x^2+1)},$$
using $x^4-x^3-x+1=(x-1)(x^3-1)=(x-1)^2(x^2+x+1)$.

Now $a+b\le-\frac12$ is equivalent (multiply by $-2x(x^2+1)$, which is negative, and reverse the inequality) to
$$2a(x-1)^2(x^2+x+1)+2x^2\ge x^3+x\iff 2a(x-1)^2(x^2+x+1)\ge x(x-1)^2 .$$
If $x=1$ this is an equality. If $x\ne1$ it reads $2a(x^2+x+1)\ge x$, which is true because $2a>1$ gives $2a(x^2+x+1)>x^2+x+1>x$.

So $a+b\le-\frac12$ whenever a positive root exists, with equality exactly when $x=1$ is a root. The value is attained: $x=1$ is a root iff $2a+2b+1=0$, e.g. $a=1$, $b=-\frac32$ gives $1-\frac32+1-\frac32+1=0$.

**Answer:** $-\frac12$.

vtrmc-1994-04.title: Substitute $t=x+\frac1x$
vtrmc-1994-04.body:
Divide by $x^2$: $a\left(x^2+\frac1{x^2}\right)+b\left(x+\frac1x\right)+1=0$. With $t=x+\frac1x\ge2$ (AM-GM, $t=2$ iff $x=1$) we have $x^2+\frac1{x^2}=t^2-2$, so $b=-\frac{a(t^2-2)+1}{t}$ and
$$a+b=\frac{-a(t^2-t-2)-1}{t}=\frac{-a(t-2)(t+1)-1}{t}.$$
For $t=2$ this is $-\frac12$ for every $a$. For $t>2$ it is decreasing in $a$, so with $a>\frac12$ it is less than its value at $a=\frac12$, which is $\frac{-(t^2-t-2)-2}{2t}=\frac{1-t}{2}<-\frac12$. Hence the maximum is $-\frac12$ (attained with $x=1$, e.g. $a=1$, $b=-\frac32$). A numerical search over $a\in(\frac12,5]$, $t\in[2,20]$ agrees.

**Answer:** $-\frac12$.

vtrmc-1994-05.title: Alternating sum over a block
vtrmc-1994-05.body:
Write $S(i,j)=f(i,j)+f(i+1,j)+f(i,j+1)+f(i+1,j+1)$; by hypothesis $S(i,j)=0$ for all $i,j$.

**An identity.** Fix $k\ge1$ and add up the unit-square relations over the $k\times k$ block with signs:
$$0=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(-1)^{i+j}S(i,j).$$
The point $(p,q)$ with $0\le p,q\le k$ appears in $S(i,j)$ exactly for $i\in\{p-1,p\}\cap[0,k-1]$ and $j\in\{q-1,q\}\cap[0,k-1]$, so its coefficient is
$$\Bigl(\sum_{i\in\{p-1,p\}\cap[0,k-1]}(-1)^i\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{j\in\{q-1,q\}\cap[0,k-1]}(-1)^j\Bigr).$$
If $1\le p\le k-1$, the first factor is $(-1)^{p-1}+(-1)^p=0$; similarly for $q$. So only the four corners survive, with coefficients $1$ for $(0,0)$, $(-1)^{k-1}$ for $(k,0)$ and $(0,k)$, and $(-1)^{2(k-1)}=1$ for $(k,k)$:
$$f(0,0)+(-1)^{k-1}\bigl(f(k,0)+f(0,k)\bigr)+f(k,k)=0 .$$
With $f(0,0)=1$ this becomes
$$1=(-1)^k\bigl(f(k,0)+f(0,k)\bigr)-f(k,k).$$

**Conclusion.** By the triangle inequality $1\le|f(k,0)|+|f(0,k)|+|f(k,k)|$, so at least one of the three points $(k,0),(0,k),(k,k)$ satisfies $|f|\ge\frac13$. For different $k\ge1$ these triples of points are disjoint, so we obtain infinitely many pairs $(m,n)$ with $|f(m,n)|\ge\frac13$. ∎

vtrmc-1994-05.title: Describe all solutions
vtrmc-1994-05.body:
Every function of the form $f(m,n)=(-1)^na(m)+(-1)^mb(n)$ satisfies the relation (the $a$-terms cancel in pairs along each column pair, the $b$-terms along each row pair). Conversely every solution has this form: the relation determines $f(m+1,n+1)$ from $f(m,n),f(m+1,n),f(m,n+1)$ (and similarly in the other directions), so $f$ is determined by its values on the row $n=0$ and the column $m=0$. Given $f$, choose $a(m)=f(m,0)$ and $b(n)=f(0,n)-(-1)^nf(0,0)$; then $b(0)=0$, so the formula gives $a(m)=f(m,0)$ on the row and $(-1)^nf(0,0)+b(n)=f(0,n)$ on the column, hence it agrees with $f$ everywhere (any one of the four values in a unit square is determined by the other three, so $f$ is determined by its row and column).

Then $f(0,0)=a(0)+b(0)=1$, and for $k\ge1$
$$f(k,0)=a(k)+(-1)^kb(0),\quad f(0,k)=(-1)^ka(0)+b(k),\quad f(k,k)=(-1)^k\bigl(a(k)+b(k)\bigr),$$
so $(-1)^k\bigl(f(k,0)+f(0,k)\bigr)-f(k,k)=a(0)+b(0)=1$, the same identity as before, and the conclusion follows in the same way. ∎

vtrmc-1994-06.title: Subtract the right multiple of $\alpha$
vtrmc-1994-06.body:
We show that every eigenvector $\beta$ with $A\beta=\beta$ is a scalar multiple of $\alpha$.

**Real $\beta$.** Suppose $\beta\in\mathbb R^n$, $A\beta=\beta$, and $\beta$ is not a multiple of $\alpha$. Since all $\alpha_i>0$ we may set
$$s=\min_{1\le i\le n}\frac{\beta_i}{\alpha_i},\qquad\gamma=\beta-s\alpha .$$
Then:
- $\gamma_i=\alpha_i\left(\frac{\beta_i}{\alpha_i}-s\right)\ge0$ for all $i$, and $\gamma_j=0$ for an index $j$ where the minimum is attained;
- $\gamma\ne0$, since otherwise $\beta=s\alpha$;
- $A\gamma=A\beta-sA\alpha=\beta-s\alpha=\gamma$.

Pick $l$ with $\gamma_l>0$. Since all entries of $A$ are positive,
$$\gamma_j=(A\gamma)_j=\sum_{k=1}^nA_{jk}\gamma_k\ge A_{jl}\gamma_l>0,$$
contradicting $\gamma_j=0$. Hence every real eigenvector for $1$ is a multiple of $\alpha$.

**Complex $\beta$.** If $\beta\in\mathbb C^n$ and $A\beta=\beta$, then, $A$ being real, $A(\operatorname{Re}\beta)=\operatorname{Re}\beta$ and $A(\operatorname{Im}\beta)=\operatorname{Im}\beta$. By the real case $\operatorname{Re}\beta=c_1\alpha$ and $\operatorname{Im}\beta=c_2\alpha$, so $\beta=(c_1+ic_2)\alpha$.

So the eigenspace of $A$ for the eigenvalue $1$ is spanned by $\alpha$: there is no eigenvector for $1$ linearly independent of $\alpha$. ∎

*(This is the hint's idea: with $c=\min\alpha_i/|\beta_i|$ one compares $\alpha$ with $c\beta$; subtracting the extremal multiple produces a nonnegative fixed vector with a zero entry, which positivity of $A$ rules out. It is a special case of the Perron–Frobenius theorem.)*

vtrmc-1994-07.title: Solve the linear recurrence for $f(n)^2$
vtrmc-1994-07.body:
Let $a_n=f(n)^2$. Squaring the definition gives the linear recurrence
$$a_{n+1}=4a_n+4n,\qquad a_1=1 .$$
- The homogeneous recurrence $a_{n+1}=4a_n$ has solutions $C\cdot4^n$.
- Try a particular solution $An+B$: $A(n+1)+B=4An+4B+4n$ gives $A=4A+4$ and $A+B=4B$, i.e. $A=-\frac43$, $B=-\frac49$.

So $a_n=C\cdot4^n-\frac{4n}{3}-\frac49$, and $a_1=1$ gives $4C=1+\frac43+\frac49=\frac{25}9$, $C=\frac{25}{36}$:
$$a_n=\frac{25\cdot4^n}{36}-\frac{4n}{3}-\frac49 .$$
(Check: $a_2=8=f(2)^2$ since $f(2)=2\sqrt2$.) Summing, with $\sum_{n=1}^N4^n=\frac{4(4^N-1)}{3}$ and $\sum n=\frac{N(N+1)}2$:
$$\sum_{n=1}^Nf(n)^2=\frac{25(4^N-1)}{27}-\frac{2N(N+1)}{3}-\frac{4N}{9}=\frac{25(4^N-1)}{27}-\frac{2N^2}{3}-\frac{10N}{9}.$$
(Check: $N=2$ gives $\frac{125}{9}-\frac{24}{9}-\frac{20}9=9=1+8$; a direct computation also agrees for $N=5$ and $N=11$.)

vtrmc-1994-07.title: Sum the recurrence directly
vtrmc-1994-07.body:
Let $S=\sum_{n=1}^Na_n$ with $a_n=f(n)^2$, $a_{n+1}=4a_n+4n$. Summing the recurrence for $n=1,\dots,N$:
$$S-a_1+a_{N+1}=4S+2N(N+1)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad S=\frac{a_{N+1}-1-2N(N+1)}{3}.$$
With the closed form $a_{N+1}=\frac{25\cdot4^{N+1}}{36}-\frac{4(N+1)}3-\frac49=\frac{25\cdot4^N}{9}-\frac{4N}{3}-\frac{16}{9}$:
$$S=\frac13\left(\frac{25\cdot4^N}{9}-\frac{25}{9}-2N^2-\frac{10N}{3}\right)=\frac{25(4^N-1)}{27}-\frac{2N^2}3-\frac{10N}9 .$$

vtrmc-1994-08.title: The sequence has period 6
vtrmc-1994-08.body:
By induction all $x_n$ are positive rationals, so the recurrence makes sense. Applying it twice,
$$x_{n+3}=\frac{19x_{n+2}}{94x_{n+1}}=\frac{19}{94x_{n+1}}\cdot\frac{19x_{n+1}}{94x_n}=\frac{19^2}{94^2x_n}.$$
Applying this twice, $x_{n+6}=\dfrac{19^2}{94^2x_{n+3}}=x_n$. Hence $x_{6n}=x_0=10$ for all $n$ and
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{x_{6n}}{2^n}=10\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac1{2^n}=20 .$$
(Exact computation: $x_0,\dots,x_6=10,\ 29,\ \frac{551}{940},\ \frac{361}{88360},\ \frac{361}{256244},\ \frac{95}{1363},\ 10$.)

**Answer:** $20$.
